report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Interoception is increasingly implicated in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet clinical translation remains limited by construct conflation, dependence on cardiac tasks, and uncertainty about whether atypical bodily processing reflects a stable deficit or a context-sensitive process.
Methods.

This critical narrative review integrates AUD-specific behavioral, psychophysiological, neuroimaging, alcohol-administration, and intervention evidence using an explicit hierarchy that separates direct interoceptive measures from mechanistic and translational support.

Direct studies indicate that lower cardiac-task performance can coexist with heightened subjective bodily attention, while recent validity work shows that heartbeat-counting scores cannot be treated as pure indices of bodily-signal detection.

Acute alcohol, stress-cue, and ambulatory findings further indicate that the behavioral significance of bodily signals depends on how they are generated, attributed, and linked to alcohol-related action.
The central clinical proposition is not to increase bodily awareness indiscriminately, but to improve the detection, differentiation, attribution, and appraisal of bodily states within context.
This signal-context-action framework generates testable hypotheses for assessment, relapse monitoring, and treatment matching within established AUD care.

Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains a major clinical challenge because craving, impaired control, stress sensitivity, negative affect, alcohol-cue reactivity, and relapse vulnerability can converge to sustain drinking despite adverse consequences (Grundinger et al., 2022; Bach et al., 2024; Harkki et al., 2025).

This clinically oriented critical narrative review was designed to address a translational question that is not resolved by descriptive evidence alone: whether interoceptive processes can improve understanding, assessment, and formulation of AUD when construct validity, contextual dependence, and evidentiary directness are considered together.

A narrative design was selected because the relevant evidence spans behavioral tasks, self-report measures, psychophysiology, neuroimaging, alcohol-administration paradigms, preclinical work, and clinical interventions, making analytical integration across levels of analysis more appropriate than pooled effect estimation.
Literature identification was conducted iteratively through PubMed/MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, with the final update conducted in September 2026.
Prior syntheses were reviewed to define the incremental question and identify areas in which newer evidence altered earlier interpretations.

Searches combined alcohol-related terms, including "alcohol use disorder," "alcohol dependence," "heavy drinking," and "binge drinking," with terms related to interoception, body perception, interoceptive accuracy, interoceptive sensibility, metacognition, cardiac tasks, interoceptive beliefs, heart-rate variability, autonomic regulation, the insula, salience networks, craving, withdrawal, cue reactivity, body-oriented therapy, mindfulness, and relapse.
Reference lists of relevant papers were also screened to identify studies that clarified core constructs, mechanisms, or clinical implications.
Evidence was organized according to directness of inference.

Greatest interpretive weight was assigned to studies that directly measured interoceptive constructs in people with AUD, followed by alcohol-administration studies that examined state-dependent bodily processing.
Neuroimaging and autonomic studies were treated as mechanistic or physiological support rather than direct measurements of interoception.

Mixed-substance, non-AUD, preclinical, and intervention studies were retained when they clarified a mechanism or translational hypothesis that could not be addressed by the AUD-specific interoception literature alone.
Interpretive weight also considered construct validity, sample relevance, temporal ordering, study design, and convergence across methods.
The synthesis was organized around interoceptive constructs, neurobiological and psychophysiological mechanisms, clinical implications, evidentiary boundaries, and future research priorities.

Particular attention was given to separating interoceptive accuracy, interoceptive sensibility, and metacognitive awareness because conflating these dimensions can convert differences in task performance, subjective attention, and confidence into an undifferentiated claim of impaired interoception.
Heartbeat-counting paradigms received additional scrutiny because their validity directly affects the inference that bodily-signal detection is reduced in AUD.
